newsitem.title: FRANCE: Juppe clears way for Mitterrand bugging probe.
newsitem.headline: Juppe clears way for Mitterrand bugging probe.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe yielded on Tuesday to pressure to lift official secrecy over widespread telephone bugging under late president Francois Mitterrand.

Juppe decided that copious files uncovered recently by the security services would be handed over to an investigating magistrate if experts determined the wiretaps had been carried out illegally, his office said.

The announcement appeared to clear the way for the judge probing illegal bugging between 1982 and 1986 to have access to files on many of the estimated 2,000 targets bugged by Mitterrand's anti-terror unit, including lawyers, politicians, journalists and actors.
The Gaullist prime minister had come under pressure from both left and right, as well as from some of the defendants, to lift secrecy on the eavesdropping, which has prompted public outrage.

The newspaper Le Monde and the magazine L'Express last week published excepts from the documents showing that Mitterrand had apparently personally ordered and overseen the bugging to shield his private life, especially connected with his illegitimate daughter Mazarine.

Juppe's office said he had decided to have experts on security intercepts study files belonging to the head of Mitterrand's rogue anti-terror unit, which were discovered in February in a garage outside Paris.
"Out of concern for procedural legality, the prime minister has decided to have these documents examined by qualified experts," his office said in a statement.

Once the National Control Commission on Security Intercepts had given its opinion on the findings, "the prime minister will ask that all the documents on wiretaps which were not carried out by the interministerial communications group be handed over to the investigating magistrate without delay".
No one could use "defence secrecy" as a pretext to withhold any document which was not strictly legal, the statement said.

The announcement effectively reversed the stance Juppe took last month, when the former head of Mitterrand's private office, Gilles Menage, wrote to ask him to lift secrecy so he could prepare his defence in equitable conditions.
At the time, the prime minister said he was unable to do so on national security grounds.

That triggered widespread criticism, including from many of Juppe's fellow Gaullists, who could not understand why the conservative premier should protect the former Socialist head of state from belated public opprobrium.

Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin, anxious to distance his party from the seamy side of Mitterrand's 14-year rule, joined the chorus urging Juppe to waive state secrecy so justice could be done.
